situation.text: Hoje você conhece Marco, de Los Angeles. Pedir almoço e escolher o recheio.

pages.goal: Hoje você aprende a pedir a conta com Check, please! e a dividir com Let’s split it, depois de uma torta.
pages.think: Pedir almoço e escolher o recheio.

pages.hook: At an American sandwich counter, you make many small choices: bread, cheese, vegetables and a side. Learn the questions and answers so you can order lunch quickly.
pages.polite: Answer each question with a short choice and **please**: **Wheat, please.** At the end, say **Thanks!**

mythfact.s: At a sandwich shop, you can choose your bread.
mythfact.why: The server asks: white, wheat or another bread.

mythfact.s: In the USA, “chips” are hot potato sticks.
mythfact.why: In the USA, “chips” are thin potato slices in a bag; hot sticks are “fries”.

mythfact.s: Many restaurants give you a box for your leftovers.
mythfact.why: You can ask, “Can I get a box, please?”

mythfact.s: The price on the menu usually includes tax.
mythfact.why: In most US states, sales tax is added at the register.

mythfact.s: You can say “Check, please!” to ask for the bill.
mythfact.why: In the USA, the bill at a restaurant is called the check.

decode.q: How much is a turkey sandwich with cheese and a soda?

compare.br: In Brazil, lunch is often a hot meal of rice, beans and meat, sometimes a self-service “por quilo” restaurant.
compare.us: In the USA, lunch is often a sandwich, a salad or a quick meal, and it is shorter. You build it with questions and choices.
compare.tip: Do not say “yes” to every question; choose: “Wheat, please.”
compare.ask: What is your favorite lunch? Say it in English.

quiz.q: Marco asks, “White or wheat bread?” You say…
What do you say to ask for the bill?
quiz.why: Check, please! is the usual phrase.
It is a choice of side dish.

pages.title: Cultural spotlight
Reading quest — Lunch in Los Angeles
text: Today I am in **Los Angeles**, and it is lunchtime. My friends say, “**Let’s grab lunch!** I know **a great spot**.” We walk to a small sandwich shop near the beach.

The line is short. A man behind the counter says, “Hi! What can I get you?” I say, “**Can I have** a turkey sandwich?” “**White or wheat?**” “Wheat, please.” “**Any cheese? Lettuce? Tomato?**” “Yes, all of them.” “**Fries or a salad?**” “A salad, please.” Then he says, “**Enjoy your lunch!**”
My friend Mia orders chicken, and Ben orders a cheese sandwich. It is not expensive, and it is **super tasty**. We sit outside and eat in the sun.

The comic “Check, Please!” by Ngozi Ukazu started in 2013. In it, a college student called Eric loves to bake, joins a hockey team and makes new friends. The title is a joke: a “check” is a hockey move, and “Check, please!” is also what you say at a restaurant.
After lunch, I say, “**Check, please!**” and the waiter brings the bill. We **split the check**. It is easy: everybody pays for their own food. I leave a small tip, and we walk to the beach.
